source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 5 (courseware unit 23): business analytics as a management tool

facts.statement: Business analytics (courseware): business analytics (BA) is the combination of skills, technologies and practices used to analyse an organisation data and performance to gain insights and make data-driven decisions in the future, with statistical analysis a common method. Its objective is to find which datasets are valuable and can boost revenue, productivity and efficiency. It can be used to predict future events related to customer activity and market trends. Most commonly it is used to analyse data from many sources (cloud applications, marketing automation, customer relationship software); to find patterns with complex statistical methods and so predict trends and behaviour; to monitor key performance indicators (KPIs) in real time; and to back decisions with the most recent facts. There is no single most important approach; the choice depends on the final aim.

Four types of analytics (courseware): applied in succession from the least to the most complicated. Descriptive analytics interprets historical data and KPIs to find patterns and trends, using data aggregation and data mining (what has happened). Diagnostic analytics focuses on past performance to understand which factors drive trends, using drill-down, data discovery, data mining and correlation, then classification and regression algorithms to find the likelihood of an event and the reasons (why it happened). Predictive analytics applies statistical models and machine learning techniques to estimate future outcomes (what is likely to happen); sales and marketing teams use it, for example, to forecast customer opinions from social media data. Prescriptive analytics uses data on previous performance to recommend how similar situations should be managed, not only forecasting results but suggesting the actions that lead to the best outcome, often using deep learning and sophisticated neural networks; it matches solutions to the immediate requirements of a customer.

Elements of business analytics (courseware): five elements are data mining, text mining, data aggregation, forecasting and data visualisation. Data mining is the search through big data sets to find patterns and relationships; it is a step in knowledge discovery in databases (KDD), and the two terms are related but different. Its results feed business intelligence, advanced analytics and real-time analytics, and help marketing, advertising, sales, customer support, production, supply chain, finance and human resources, including fraud prevention, risk management and cybersecurity planning.

Data mining process and techniques (courseware): four steps. (1) Data collection: identify the relevant data and compile it from source systems, a data warehouse or a data lake (a repository for structured and unstructured data); external data may be used. (2) Data preparation: explore, profile and pre-process the data and cleanse it to correct errors and quality issues, and convert it to keep data sets consistent. (3) The mining: choose a technique and apply algorithms, often trained first on smaller samples. (4) Interpretation and analysis: findings are built into analytical models for decisions and explained to business users through data visualisation and storytelling. Techniques: association rules (if-then statements that show links between data elements, with support, the frequency with which related elements appear, and confidence, the number of times the if-then statement is accurate); classification (assign data to categories: decision trees, naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbour, logistic regression); clustering (group data with common characteristics: k-means, hierarchical, Gaussian mixture); regression (predict values from relationships among variables: linear and multivariate regression); sequence and path analysis (patterns in which one event leads to later ones); and neural networks (modelled on the human brain; deep learning is a more advanced subfield, helpful in pattern recognition). Pattern recognition and anomaly detection (finding outliers) are common use cases.

Benefits and uses of data mining (courseware): benefits are more productivity in marketing and sales (better targeted campaigns and higher conversion), better customer service (spotting problems early), better supply chain management (demand projections and stock levels), higher production uptime (predictive maintenance from sensor data), stronger risk management and lower costs. Industry examples: retail (recommendation engines from clickstream data and inventory management), financial services (risk models, fraud detection, loan and credit application validation, upselling), insurance (pricing and risk modelling), manufacturing (uptime and operational efficiency), entertainment (personalised suggestions) and healthcare (diagnosis, treatment, medical imaging analysis).

Text mining (courseware): text mining, or text data mining, converts unstructured text into a structured format to find patterns and insights using methods such as naive Bayes, support vector machines and deep learning. Data types: structured data (standardised tabular format, such as names, addresses, phone numbers), unstructured data (no standard format: social media, reviews, video and audio) and semi-structured data (partly organised but not fit for a relational database, such as XML, JSON and HTML). Most data in the world is unstructured, which makes text mining useful. Text pre-processing cleans the text first (language identification, tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, chunking, syntax parsing). Information retrieval (IR) locates and delivers pertinent documents for queries: tokenisation separates text into tokens (words and sentences) used as bag-of-words in models; stemming strips prefixes and suffixes to the root form, reducing the space needed for indexing. Natural language processing (NLP) has subtasks: summarisation (condensing text), part-of-speech tagging (labelling each token as noun, verb and so on), text categorisation (classifying documents into predefined topics) and sentiment analysis (identifying positive or negative sentiment about brands, products and services). Information extraction (IE) has subtasks: feature selection (choosing the dimensions that contribute most to a predictive model), feature extraction (choosing a subset of features to improve a classification task) and named-entity recognition (finding and classifying entities such as names and places).

Data aggregation (courseware): data aggregation is collecting raw data and presenting it in summary form (average, lowest, maximum, sum and count) over a period for statistical analysis. Time aggregation: all data points for a single resource over a time period. Spatial aggregation: all data points for a group of resources over a time period. Reporting terms: time frame for reports (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly); granularity (the time period over which individual data points are gathered and aggregated; for example five-minute granularity averages the points over five minutes, from one minute to a month or more); and polling period (how often a resource is sampled for data). If the polling period equals the granularity, one value per resource is averaged; if the polling period is shorter, several samples are taken and averaged.

Forecasting (courseware): forecasting is predicting what will happen by taking account of what has happened and what is happening; it is a decision-making tool for planning and budgeting. Qualitative (judging) methods rest on expert opinion and intuition and are subjective, so the forecast may contain errors; quantitative methods use mathematical procedures and large volumes of data, are consistent and objective, and are used by most firms for planning and budgeting. Features: forecasts involve future events, cover recent and historical occurrences and use various techniques. Process: establish a foundation for future projections (where the company stands); formulate projections for the company business (investigate and estimate the future conditions of the industry); make adjustments (compare earlier forecasts with actual results and analyse the differences); and look back at the steps, with a check after each and tweaks. The courseware notes that sales forecasting is an iterative process.

Data visualisation (courseware): data visualisation represents data through charts, plots, infographics and animation so that complex relationships are easy to grasp. Four functions: idea generation (brainstorming), idea illustration (such as Gantt and waterfall charts to describe workflows), visual discovery (finding patterns in a dataset) and everyday dataviz (communicating data to colleagues). Common forms in dashboards: tables (a grid for comparing variables, which can overwhelm); pie and stacked bar charts (show proportions of a total); line graphs and area charts (change over time); histograms (distribution of numbers, bars with no gaps); scatter plots (relationship between two variables; bubble charts add a third variable as bubble size); heat maps (behaviour by location or range); and tree maps (hierarchical data as nested rectangles comparing proportions of categories).

Excel proficiency (courseware): skills named are spreadsheets, workbooks, formulas, data linking, pivot tables, charts, data analytics, macros and automation, IF statements and data validation; proficiency means being able to create functions, pivot tables and charts.

Big data analytics (courseware): big data analytics applies advanced analytical methods to very large, diverse data sets (structured, semi-structured and unstructured, from many sources, from terabytes to zettabytes). Big data is described by high volume, velocity and variety (or diversity) at once; it is too large or complex for traditional relational databases to record, manage or process in a timely way. Sources include sensors, devices, video, networks, logs, transactional applications, the web and social media. Techniques: text analytics, machine learning, predictive analytics, data mining, statistics and natural language processing. Uses: improving customer integration (a complete view from many touch points), detecting and minimising fraud (real-time monitoring of transactions), and improving supply chain efficiency (tracking items and finding inefficiencies). Industry uses: manufacturing (predictive maintenance, operational effectiveness, production optimisation), retail (product development, customer experience, customer lifetime value, in-store experience, pricing), healthcare (genomic research, patient experience, claims fraud, billing), oil and gas (equipment maintenance, exploration, production optimisation), telecommunications (network capacity, customer churn, new offers) and financial services (fraud and compliance, innovation, anti-money laundering, regulatory reporting).

Importance and workings of big data analytics (courseware): benefits are reducing cost (for example storing data in a cloud-based data lake), faster and better decisions (using in-memory analytics and streaming data from internet of things sensors) and developing new products and services. Workflow: collection (from cloud storage, mobile applications and in-store sensors; data warehouses for structured data and data lakes for data that is too diverse); processing (batch processing handles large blocks over a period when a longer turnaround is acceptable; stream processing handles small batches at once for quick results, more complex and costly); cleaning (correct formatting and removal of redundant or irrelevant data, since bad data misleads); and analysis (data mining finding patterns and clusters and outliers, predictive analytics forecasting from the past, and deep learning imitating human learning patterns).

Big data tools and challenges (courseware): Hadoop is an open-source framework storing and analysing large datasets on clusters of commodity hardware, structured and unstructured; NoSQL databases are non-relational and do not require a fixed schema, suiting large volumes of raw unstructured data; MapReduce distributes data to different nodes in a cluster (mapping) and organises and condenses the results from each node (reducing); YARN manages job scheduling and resources in the cluster; Spark is an open-source cluster computing framework handling batch and stream processing quickly; Tableau is a self-service visual analytics platform. Challenges: making big data accessible; maintaining data quality (checking for mistakes, inconsistencies, conflicts and duplicates); data security and privacy (compliance and tightly established data processes); and identifying appropriate tools and platforms that are compatible with the existing ecosystem and flexible.

Web and mobile analytics (courseware): web analytics studies visitor behaviour on websites; mobile web analytics collects data from customers who visit a website using mobile phones and helps determine which aspects work best for mobile traffic; mobile analytics data include page views, visits, users, countries and mobile-specific information (device model, manufacturer, screen resolution, capabilities, service provider and language). Tracking problems: visitor identification (the hardest; cookies and JavaScript are unreliable on mobile devices); JavaScript page tagging (assumes the browser runs JavaScript); HTTP cookies (can be disabled); image tags; and IP address (the gateway address may reveal the operator and country but not the user). Collection methods: packet sniffing (tagless data capture), image tags or beacons, link redirection (records clicks from marketing and clicks leaving a site), HTTP header analysis (with a device database), IP address analysis and gateway logs. Comparison: web analytics traditionally measured page views but has grown to new, repeat and unique users and cohorts; mobile analytics focuses on app use (length of visits, origin of visitors, in-app purchases) and adds the location of the user; sessions on mobile are shorter and more frequent; advertising and ad-blocking work differently; users move between devices, so a customised approach across platforms is needed.

Importance, benefits, challenges and skills of business analytics (courseware): four reasons it matters: it boosts performance by showing what is working, enables quicker and more accurate choices, reduces the likelihood of negative outcomes and inspires change and creativity. Benefits: preparing for unforeseen circumstances by modelling and projecting trends in sales and earnings, testing new marketing initiatives, forecasting order volume and reducing waste, and finding customers unlikely to return. Challenges: need for full support from leadership and a clear strategy; buy-in from senior management; IT engagement and the right technology and tools; executive ownership and collaboration of business and IT; sustained dedication in the first months, as the cost may be high and returns slow; involvement of end-users and change management; difficulty integrating varied data; and a shortage of skilled staff and data storage limits for smaller organisations. Skills: critical thinking, problem solving, communication, curiosity and attention to detail.

payload.title: What business analytics is and what it is used for
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Business analytics (BA)** is the mix of **skills, technologies and practices** used to **analyse an organisation data and performance**, gain **insights** and make **data-driven decisions**, often by **statistical analysis**.

**Aim:** find which **datasets are valuable** and can raise **revenue, productivity and efficiency**; predict **customer activity** and **market trends**.

**Typical uses:**

- Analyse data from **many sources** (cloud applications, marketing automation, CRM).
- Find **patterns** with complex statistical methods to **predict trends**.
- Watch **key performance indicators (KPIs)** in real time.
- Back decisions with the **most recent facts**.

No single approach is always best; the choice depends on the **final aim**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Analytics turns stored data into a basis for decisions.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the objective of business analytics?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To find which datasets are valuable and use them to improve revenue, productivity and efficiency.

payload.title: The four types of analytics
payload.core_explanation_md:
Applied **in succession** from the simplest to the most complex:

| Type | Question | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Descriptive** | **What happened?** | Interpret **historical data and KPIs**; **aggregation and data mining** |
| **Diagnostic** | **Why did it happen?** | **Drill-down, data discovery, data mining, correlation**; then **classification and regression** to find likelihood and reasons |
| **Predictive** | **What is likely to happen?** | **Statistical models and machine learning** to estimate future outcomes (for example forecasting client opinions from social media) |
| **Prescriptive** | **What should we do?** | Recommend **actions** for the best outcome, often with **deep learning and neural networks**; matches solutions to a **customer immediate needs** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each type builds on the one before it: describe, explain, predict, recommend.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of analytics recommends the action to take?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Prescriptive analytics.

payload.title: Data mining: process and techniques
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Data mining** searches **big datasets** for **patterns and relationships**; it is a step in **knowledge discovery in databases (KDD)**. Its results feed **business intelligence, advanced and real-time analytics**, and help marketing, sales, support, production, supply chain, finance and HR, including **fraud prevention, risk management and cybersecurity planning**.

**Four steps:** 1) **data collection** (source systems, **data warehouse** or **data lake**); 2) **data preparation** (explore, profile, **cleanse**, make consistent); 3) **the mining** (choose a technique; algorithms often **trained on small samples first**); 4) **interpretation** (build into models; explain through **visualisation and storytelling**).

| Technique | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Association rules** | **If-then** links; **support** = how often the elements appear together; **confidence** = how often the if-then holds |
| **Classification** | Assign data to **categories** (decision trees, naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbour, logistic regression) |
| **Clustering** | Group data with **common characteristics** (k-means, hierarchical, Gaussian mixture) |
| **Regression** | **Predict values** from relationships between variables |
| **Sequence and path analysis** | Patterns where **one event leads to later ones** |
| **Neural networks** | **Brain-like models**; **deep learning** is an advanced subfield for **pattern recognition** |

**Anomaly detection** finds **outliers**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A data lake holds raw data of all kinds; a warehouse holds organised data.

self_check.prompt_text: What do support and confidence measure for an association rule?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Support is how often the elements appear together; confidence is how often the if-then statement is accurate.

payload.title: Support and confidence of an association rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
For a rule **if A then B**:

**Support = transactions containing both A and B / all transactions.**

**Confidence = transactions containing both A and B / transactions containing A.**

Example pattern: of **200 transactions**, **40** contain A and **30** contain both; support = **30 / 200 = 15 per cent**, confidence = **30 / 40 = 75 per cent**.

A rule with **high support** is common; one with **high confidence** is reliable when A occurs.

variables.name: Transactions containing both A and B

assumptions: A is present in at least one transaction
common_errors: Dividing by all transactions for confidence

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Support measures frequency; confidence measures how often the rule holds.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the denominator of confidence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The number of transactions containing A, the if part of the rule.

payload.title: Text mining and its techniques
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Text mining** turns **unstructured text into structured form** to find patterns, using **naive Bayes, support vector machines and deep learning**.

| Data type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Structured** | **Standard tabular** format (names, addresses, phone numbers) |
| **Unstructured** | **No standard format** (social media, reviews, video, audio) |
| **Semi-structured** | **Partly organised**, not fit for a relational database (XML, JSON, HTML) |

**Pre-processing:** language identification, **tokenisation**, **part-of-speech tagging**, chunking, syntax parsing.

**Information retrieval (IR):** find and deliver the pertinent documents. **Tokenisation** splits text into **tokens** (bag-of-words); **stemming** strips prefixes and suffixes to the **root**, saving index space.

**Natural language processing (NLP):** **summarisation**, **part-of-speech tagging**, **text categorisation** (classify by topic) and **sentiment analysis** (positive or negative opinion).

**Information extraction (IE):** **feature selection** (dimensions that matter most for a model), **feature extraction** (a subset of features to improve classification) and **named-entity recognition** (find names and places).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Most data in the world is unstructured, which is why text mining matters.

self_check.prompt_text: What does stemming do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It strips prefixes and suffixes from words to reach the root form, reducing index space.

payload.title: Data aggregation: time, space, granularity and polling
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Aggregation** collects raw data and **summarises** it (**average, minimum, maximum, sum, count**) for analysis.

- **Time aggregation:** all data points for **one resource** over a period.
- **Spatial aggregation:** all data points for a **group of resources** over a period.

**Terms:** **time frame** of a report (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly); **granularity** (the **period over which points are aggregated**, for example five minutes); **polling period** (**how often a resource is sampled**).

If the **polling period equals the granularity**, each resource gives **one value** per period. If the polling period is **shorter**, several samples are **averaged** within the granularity.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Coarser granularity gives fewer, smoother data points.

self_check.prompt_text: What is granularity in data aggregation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The time period over which individual data points are gathered and aggregated.

payload.title: Forecasting: methods, features and process
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forecasting** predicts the future from **what has happened and is happening**, for **planning and budgeting**.

| Qualitative (judging) | Quantitative |
| --- | --- |
| **Expert opinion and intuition** | **Mathematical procedures** and **large volumes of data** |
| **Subjective**; error-prone | **Consistent and objective** |

**Features:** involves **future events**; covers **recent and historical** occurrences; uses **various techniques**.

**Process:** 1) set a **foundation** (where the firm stands); 2) **formulate projections** (study the industry and estimate the future); 3) **adjust** (compare earlier forecasts with actual results and analyse differences); 4) **look back**: check each step and tweak. Sales forecasting is an **iterative** process.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Comparing forecasts with outcomes is how the method improves.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can qualitative forecasts be unreliable?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They rest on personal judgement and intuition, which are subjective and may contain errors.

payload.title: Simple forecasting arithmetic
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Moving average forecast = average of the last n periods.** Example: sales of **100, 110, 120** give a three-period forecast of **(100 + 110 + 120) / 3 = 110**.

**Forecast error = actual - forecast.**

**Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100.**

**Simple growth forecast = last value x (1 + growth rate).**

Quantitative methods like these are **objective and repeatable**, but they assume the **past pattern continues**.

assumptions: The recent past predicts the near future
common_errors: Averaging the wrong number of periods

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A longer average smooths noise but responds more slowly to change.

self_check.prompt_text: How is a three-period moving average forecast calculated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is the average of the last three observed values.

Sources: **sensors, devices, video, networks, logs, transactions, the web, social media**.

**Techniques:** text analytics, machine learning, predictive analytics, data mining, statistics, NLP.

payload.title: Why big data analytics matters and how it works
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Benefits:** **lower cost** (for example a cloud-based **data lake**), **faster and better decisions** (**in-memory analytics**, streaming data from **internet of things** sensors) and **new products and services**.

**Workflow:**

1. **Collection**: cloud storage, apps, in-store sensors; **warehouses** for structured data, **data lakes** for diverse data.
2. **Processing**: **batch** (large blocks over a period; longer turnaround) or **stream** (small batches at once; faster, **harder and costlier**).
3. **Cleaning**: correct formats, **remove redundant or irrelevant data**; bad data misleads.
4. **Analysis**: **data mining** (patterns, clusters, outliers), **predictive analytics** (forecast from the past), **deep learning** (imitates human learning).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Choose stream processing only when decisions cannot wait for a batch.

items.title: What business analytics is and what it is used for
items.core_explanation_md:
**Business analytics (BA)** is the mix of **skills, technologies and practices** used to **analyse an organisation data and performance**, gain **insights** and make **data-driven decisions**, often by **statistical analysis**.

**Aim:** find which **datasets are valuable** and can raise **revenue, productivity and efficiency**; predict **customer activity** and **market trends**.

**Typical uses:**

- Analyse data from **many sources** (cloud applications, marketing automation, CRM).
- Find **patterns** with complex statistical methods to **predict trends**.
- Watch **key performance indicators (KPIs)** in real time.
- Back decisions with the **most recent facts**.

No single approach is always best; the choice depends on the **final aim**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Analytics turns stored data into a basis for decisions.

items.title: The four types of analytics
items.core_explanation_md:
Applied **in succession** from the simplest to the most complex:

| Type | Question | How |
| --- | --- | --- |

| **Prescriptive** | **What should we do?** | Recommend **actions** for the best outcome, often with **deep learning and neural networks**; matches solutions to a **customer immediate needs** |

items.title: Data mining: process and techniques
items.core_explanation_md:
**Data mining** searches **big datasets** for **patterns and relationships**; it is a step in **knowledge discovery in databases (KDD)**. Its results feed **business intelligence, advanced and real-time analytics**, and help marketing, sales, support, production, supply chain, finance and HR, including **fraud prevention, risk management and cybersecurity planning**.

**Four steps:** 1) **data collection** (source systems, **data warehouse** or **data lake**); 2) **data preparation** (explore, profile, **cleanse**, make consistent); 3) **the mining** (choose a technique; algorithms often **trained on small samples first**); 4) **interpretation** (build into models; explain through **visualisation and storytelling**).

| Technique | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Association rules** | **If-then** links; **support** = how often the elements appear together; **confidence** = how often the if-then holds |
| **Classification** | Assign data to **categories** (decision trees, naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbour, logistic regression) |
| **Clustering** | Group data with **common characteristics** (k-means, hierarchical, Gaussian mixture) |
| **Regression** | **Predict values** from relationships between variables |
| **Sequence and path analysis** | Patterns where **one event leads to later ones** |
| **Neural networks** | **Brain-like models**; **deep learning** is an advanced subfield for **pattern recognition** |

**Anomaly detection** finds **outliers**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A data lake holds raw data of all kinds; a warehouse holds organised data.

items.title: Support and confidence of an association rule
items.core_explanation_md:
For a rule **if A then B**:

**Support = transactions containing both A and B / all transactions.**

**Confidence = transactions containing both A and B / transactions containing A.**

Example pattern: of **200 transactions**, **40** contain A and **30** contain both; support = **30 / 200 = 15 per cent**, confidence = **30 / 40 = 75 per cent**.

A rule with **high support** is common; one with **high confidence** is reliable when A occurs.

items.title: Text mining and its techniques
items.core_explanation_md:
**Text mining** turns **unstructured text into structured form** to find patterns, using **naive Bayes, support vector machines and deep learning**.

| Data type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Structured** | **Standard tabular** format (names, addresses, phone numbers) |
| **Unstructured** | **No standard format** (social media, reviews, video, audio) |
| **Semi-structured** | **Partly organised**, not fit for a relational database (XML, JSON, HTML) |

**Pre-processing:** language identification, **tokenisation**, **part-of-speech tagging**, chunking, syntax parsing.

**Information retrieval (IR):** find and deliver the pertinent documents. **Tokenisation** splits text into **tokens** (bag-of-words); **stemming** strips prefixes and suffixes to the **root**, saving index space.

**Natural language processing (NLP):** **summarisation**, **part-of-speech tagging**, **text categorisation** (classify by topic) and **sentiment analysis** (positive or negative opinion).

**Information extraction (IE):** **feature selection** (dimensions that matter most for a model), **feature extraction** (a subset of features to improve classification) and **named-entity recognition** (find names and places).

items.title: Data aggregation: time, space, granularity and polling
items.core_explanation_md:
**Aggregation** collects raw data and **summarises** it (**average, minimum, maximum, sum, count**) for analysis.

- **Time aggregation:** all data points for **one resource** over a period.
- **Spatial aggregation:** all data points for a **group of resources** over a period.

**Terms:** **time frame** of a report (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly); **granularity** (the **period over which points are aggregated**, for example five minutes); **polling period** (**how often a resource is sampled**).

If the **polling period equals the granularity**, each resource gives **one value** per period. If the polling period is **shorter**, several samples are **averaged** within the granularity.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The time period over which individual data points are gathered and aggregated.

items.title: Forecasting: methods, features and process
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forecasting** predicts the future from **what has happened and is happening**, for **planning and budgeting**.

| Qualitative (judging) | Quantitative |
| --- | --- |
| **Expert opinion and intuition** | **Mathematical procedures** and **large volumes of data** |
| **Subjective**; error-prone | **Consistent and objective** |

**Features:** involves **future events**; covers **recent and historical** occurrences; uses **various techniques**.

**Process:** 1) set a **foundation** (where the firm stands); 2) **formulate projections** (study the industry and estimate the future); 3) **adjust** (compare earlier forecasts with actual results and analyse differences); 4) **look back**: check each step and tweak. Sales forecasting is an **iterative** process.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Comparing forecasts with outcomes is how the method improves.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can qualitative forecasts be unreliable?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They rest on personal judgement and intuition, which are subjective and may contain errors.

items.title: Simple forecasting arithmetic
items.core_explanation_md:
**Moving average forecast = average of the last n periods.** Example: sales of **100, 110, 120** give a three-period forecast of **(100 + 110 + 120) / 3 = 110**.

**Forecast error = actual - forecast.**

**Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100.**

**Simple growth forecast = last value x (1 + growth rate).**

Quantitative methods like these are **objective and repeatable**, but they assume the **past pattern continues**.

assumptions: The recent past predicts the near future
common_errors: Averaging the wrong number of periods

items.expanded_explanation_md: A longer average smooths noise but responds more slowly to change.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It is the average of the last three observed values.

items.title: Big data analytics: meaning, uses and industry examples
items.core_explanation_md:
**Big data** is data so **large or complex** that normal relational databases cannot **record, manage or process** it in time. It is described by high **volume, velocity and variety** together, and may be **structured, semi-structured or unstructured**, from **terabytes to zettabytes**. Sources: **sensors, devices, video, networks, logs, transactions, the web, social media**.

**Techniques:** text analytics, machine learning, predictive analytics, data mining, statistics, NLP.

**Uses:** a **complete view of customers**, **real-time fraud detection**, a **more efficient supply chain**.

| Industry | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Manufacturing** | **Predictive maintenance**, operational effectiveness, **production optimisation** |
| **Retail** | **Product development, customer experience, customer lifetime value, pricing** |
| **Healthcare** | **Genomic research, patient outcomes, claims fraud, billing** |
| **Oil and gas** | **Equipment maintenance, exploration, production** |
| **Telecom** | **Network capacity, customer churn, new offers** |
| **Financial services** | **Fraud and compliance, anti-money laundering, regulatory reporting, innovation** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Volume, velocity and variety are the three defining features.

items.title: Why big data analytics matters and how it works
items.core_explanation_md:
**Benefits:** **lower cost** (for example a cloud-based **data lake**), **faster and better decisions** (**in-memory analytics**, streaming data from **internet of things** sensors) and **new products and services**.

**Workflow:**

1. **Collection**: cloud storage, apps, in-store sensors; **warehouses** for structured data, **data lakes** for diverse data.
2. **Processing**: **batch** (large blocks over a period; longer turnaround) or **stream** (small batches at once; faster, **harder and costlier**).
3. **Cleaning**: correct formats, **remove redundant or irrelevant data**; bad data misleads.
4. **Analysis**: **data mining** (patterns, clusters, outliers), **predictive analytics** (forecast from the past), **deep learning** (imitates human learning).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Choose stream processing only when decisions cannot wait for a batch.

self_check.prompt_text: When is stream processing preferred to batch processing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When results are needed quickly, because it handles small batches as the data arrives.

items.title: Web and mobile analytics: tracking and comparison
items.core_explanation_md:
**Web analytics** studies visitor behaviour on websites; **mobile web analytics** collects data on visitors using **mobile phones** and shows what works best for **mobile traffic**.

**Data:** page views, visits, users, countries and **mobile-specific information** (device model, maker, screen size, capabilities, provider, language).

**Tracking problems:** **visitor identification** is the hardest (**cookies and JavaScript are unreliable** on mobile); **JavaScript tagging** assumes the browser runs it; **cookies** can be disabled; **IP address** reveals the operator or country, not the user.

**Collection methods:** **packet sniffing** (tagless), **image beacons**, **link redirection** (records clicks, including those leaving a site), **HTTP header analysis**, **IP analysis**, **gateway logs**.

| Web analytics | Mobile analytics |
| --- | --- |
| Page views, **new, repeat and unique users**, cohorts | **App use**: length of visit, origin, **in-app purchases**, **location** |
| Longer sessions | **Shorter, more frequent** sessions |
| Ads can be blocked in the browser | Ads handled **inside apps** |

Users **switch devices**, so a **cross-platform** approach is needed.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A session is the period of one visit; defining it differs between websites and apps.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is visitor identification hard in mobile analytics?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cookies and JavaScript are unreliable on mobile devices, so visitors cannot always be recognised.

items.title: Importance, benefits, challenges and skills of business analytics
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why it matters:** it **boosts performance** (shows what works), enables **quicker, more accurate choices**, **reduces negative outcomes** and **inspires change and creativity**.

**Benefits:** **model and project trends** to prepare for the unforeseen; **test new marketing**; **forecast orders and cut waste**; **find customers unlikely to return**.

**Challenges:** **leadership support and a clear strategy**; **senior management buy-in**; **IT engagement and tools**; **executive ownership**; **sustained dedication** (cost may be high and returns slow early on); **end-user involvement and change management**; **integrating varied data**; **shortage of skilled staff** and **storage limits** in small firms.

**Skills:** **critical thinking, problem solving, communication, curiosity, attention to detail**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Analytics succeeds only when the organisation is ready to act on what it learns.

self_check.expected_takeaway: For example lack of leadership buy-in and a shortage of skilled staff.
